PRUNING FILTERS FOR EFFICIENT CONVNETS.p.chunks:
Core Summary: Magnitude-based Filter Pruning (ICLR 2017)
This paper proposes a simple and effective method for accelerating convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by pruning filters based on their ℓ1-norm (sum of absolute weights). The method significantly reduces computation and parameters without introducing sparsity, making it compatible with existing high-performance BLAS libraries.

✂️ Key Method Details:
Filters, not individual weights, are pruned. Each pruned filter removes its associated feature map and corresponding kernels in the next layer, reducing total FLOPs.

ℓ1-norm is used to rank filter importance. Filters with smaller weight magnitudes are considered less important.

Supports multi-layer pruning (either one-shot or iterative), with layer-wise pruning ratios adapted via sensitivity analysis.

ResNet-compatible: The first conv layer in a residual block can be pruned freely. The second conv layer must follow the pruning pattern of the identity (shortcut) layer.

 Pruning Procedure (Per Layer):
Compute the ℓ1-norm for each filter.

Rank filters and prune the bottom m filters.

Adjust input channels and kernels in the subsequent layer accordingly.

Retraining Strategies:
One-shot pruning + retraining: suitable in most cases.

Iterative pruning + retraining: better for very deep networks or sensitive layers.

 Experimental Results (CIFAR-10 & ImageNet):
On VGG-16 (CIFAR-10), 34% FLOP reduction is achieved with minimal accuracy loss.

On ResNet-110 (CIFAR-10), 38.6% FLOP reduction with only 0.23% accuracy drop.

Training a pruned model from scratch performs worse than fine-tuning a pre-trained model.

 Advantages:
No need for sparse libraries or custom hardware.

No extra regularization or meta-parameters required.

Despite its simplicity, ℓ1-norm outperforms random or activation-based pruning in most layers.
